claims.text: A physically informed machine-learning model integrating DFT calculations, neutron scattering, and thermal-diffusivity measurements can predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional DFT-based or empirical methods.
Extreme chemical disorder and anharmonic phonon scattering are important determinants of phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
Nanocrystalline or polycrystalline high-entropy alloys have inherent compositional disorder relevant to thermal-insulation applications.
Data-driven approaches can be deployed to screen and identify promising high-entropy-alloy compositions.
A curated combination of DFT, neutron-scattering, and thermal-diffusivity data is suitable for training a model to identify alloys with intrinsically low phonon thermal conductivity.
At 600–1100 °C, anharmonic effects and disorder-induced phonon scattering dominate heat transport in the target high-entropy alloys.
The model is applicable only to compositional and microstructural features represented adequately in its training data.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder enhances phonon scattering.
Anharmonic lattice vibrations enhance phonon scattering.
A machine-learning model can learn nonlinear correlations among composition, disorder, microstructure, and phonon-dispersion characteristics.
Traditional computational methods underrepresent anharmonic phonon interactions and disorder-induced localization in high-entropy alloys.
High-entropy alloys with greater disorder will systematically be predicted to have lower phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error by approximately 10–20% relative to conventional methods.
Conventional DFT with perturbative anharmonic corrections and empirical or semi-empirical models have limited accuracy for disorder and anharmonicity in high-entropy alloys.
Predictions will be less reliable for compositions or microstructures substantially outside the training-data distribution.
The quantitative improvement depends critically on training-set representativeness and model generalization.
Laser-flash analysis or TDTR can be used to determine phonon thermal conductivity over 600–1100 °C in the proposed benchmark.
Neutron scattering can evaluate phonon dispersion and disorder-induced localization in the benchmark alloys.
A prediction error greater than 20%, or failure to rank more-disordered compositions below less-disordered compositions in thermal conductivity, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
